title: Adrenergic Antagonists
summary: Alpha and beta blockers: selectivity, clinical uses and hazards.

lessons.title: Alpha Blockers

levels.kid:
Remember the alpha-1 buttons that make blood vessels squeeze? **Alpha blockers** cover those buttons.

When the buttons are covered, blood vessels relax and get wider, so blood pressure goes down. There are also alpha buttons in the tube that carries pee out of the bladder in older men. Covering them helps the tube relax, so peeing gets easier.

One thing to watch: the first time someone takes an alpha blocker, they might feel dizzy or even faint when they stand up fast. So doctors tell people to take the first one at bedtime and get up slowly.
levels.hs:
**α blockers** stop norepinephrine from acting on α receptors.

**Selective α1 blockers** (names end in **-zosin**):
- **Prazosin**, **terazosin**, **doxazosin**: relax blood vessels → lower blood pressure; also relax the prostate and bladder neck → easier urination in **benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)**.
- **Tamsulosin**, **silodosin**, **alfuzosin**: more "uroselective" (target α1A in the prostate), so less blood pressure drop. Also used to help pass kidney stones.

**Main side effect: first-dose hypotension** — dizziness or fainting when standing, especially after the first dose or a dose increase. Taking the first dose at bedtime helps. Other effects: stuffy nose, headache, and with tamsulosin, problems during cataract surgery (**floppy iris syndrome**) and ejaculation problems.

**Nonselective α blockers** (α1 and α2):
- **Phenoxybenzamine**: binds permanently (irreversibly); used before surgery for **pheochromocytoma**, a tumor that pours out adrenaline-type hormones.
- **Phentolamine**: reversible and short-acting; used for sudden catecholamine surges and for leaked norepinephrine IVs.

Blocking α2 too removes the brake on NE release, so nonselective blockers cause more **reflex tachycardia**.

**Prazosin** is also used for trauma-related nightmares, with mixed evidence.
levels.college:
**α1 blockade** reduces arteriolar and venous tone (lower SVR and preload) and relaxes smooth muscle of the prostate capsule, bladder neck and urethra. Unlike many vasodilators, selective α1 blockers cause relatively little reflex tachycardia because presynaptic α2 inhibitory feedback is intact.

**Subtypes**: α1A predominates in the prostate, α1B in many vessels, α1D in the bladder and some vessels. Tamsulosin and silodosin (α1A-preferring) minimize blood pressure effects; silodosin is the most α1A-selective (with the highest rate of retrograde ejaculation).

**First-dose phenomenon**: postural hypotension and syncope after the first dose (venodilation with impaired orthostatic compensation), worse with volume depletion, diuretics or concurrent PDE5 inhibitors. Titrate up gradually.

**Hypertension**: α1 blockers lower pressure but are not first line. In ALLHAT, the doxazosin arm was stopped early because of more heart failure and cardiovascular events than chlorthalidone.

**Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS)**: α1A blockade of the iris dilator causes billowing iris, progressive miosis and prolapse during cataract surgery; it can persist after stopping the drug. Patients should tell the eye surgeon.

**Nonselective agents**:
- **Phenoxybenzamine** alkylates α receptors covalently: effect lasts until new receptors are made, outlasting the drug. Causes reflex tachycardia, nasal congestion, postural hypotension.
- **Phentolamine** is a competitive α1/α2 blocker: for pheochromocytoma crises, MAOI–tyramine reactions, catecholamine extravasation, and reversal of local anesthesia with epinephrine in dental soft tissue.

**Mixed α/β blockers**: labetalol and carvedilol (covered with β blockers).

**α2 antagonism** appears in mirtazapine (increasing NE and 5-HT release) and has been explored for other uses.
levels.phd:
**Covalent pharmacology.** Phenoxybenzamine is a β-haloalkylamine that cyclizes to a reactive aziridinium ion, alkylating a cysteine in the α receptor's binding pocket. Recovery depends on receptor resynthesis, with an offset of days. In receptor theory, irreversible antagonists were the tool Furchgott used to estimate agonist affinity and efficacy: partially inactivating receptors with an alkylator and comparing dose–response curves reveals the receptor reserve (spare receptors). This method underlies the operational model of agonism.

**The prostate as pharmacology.** α1A receptors mediate the dynamic component of bladder outlet obstruction (smooth muscle tone), while 5α-reductase inhibitors address the static component (gland volume). The MTOPS trial (2003) showed the combination of doxazosin and finasteride reduced clinical progression more than either alone.

**Medical expulsive therapy** for ureteral stones with tamsulosin became widespread after small trials; the large SUSPEND trial (2015) found no benefit for stones overall, while meta-analyses suggest benefit for larger distal stones. This is a lesson in how small trials and mechanism can mislead.

**Prazosin and PTSD.** Nighttime noradrenergic hyperactivity is thought to disrupt REM sleep and drive trauma nightmares. Early VA trials of prazosin showed large effects; a 2018 multicenter VA trial (Raskind) in chronically ill veterans found no benefit. Explanations include patient selection and the placebo response; guidelines now differ on its use.

**ALLHAT doxazosin**: the excess heart failure may partly reflect unmasking of heart failure that chlorthalidone treated, rather than direct harm, but the early stop ended α1 blockers' role as first-line antihypertensives.

**Raynaud and α2C**: cold-induced vasoconstriction in the fingers is partly mediated by α2C receptors translocating to the cell surface, which may explain the limited effect of α1 blockers in Raynaud phenomenon.
levels.expert:
**Practical α-blocker reasoning.**

**Older man on tamsulosin falls at night**: postural hypotension plus nocturia is a classic fall mechanism. Review timing, combined antihypertensives, PDE5 inhibitors and volume status. Falls in older adults are a major cause of subdural hematomas, so this is a neurosurgical problem too.

**Autonomic failure** (Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, diabetic autonomic neuropathy): α1 blockers given for BPH can unmask severe orthostatic hypotension. Ask about lightheadedness on standing before prescribing.

**Cataract surgery**: always ask about current or past tamsulosin before eye surgery; the surgeon can prepare iris hooks or pharmacologic strategies for IFIS.

**Autonomic dysreflexia** after spinal cord injury at or above T6: a noxious stimulus below the lesion (full bladder, blocked catheter, constipation, pressure sore) triggers massive unopposed sympathetic vasoconstriction with severe hypertension, headache, flushing above the lesion and reflex bradycardia. First: sit the patient up, loosen clothing, find and remove the trigger (check the catheter). If pressure stays high, give a fast-acting antihypertensive; topical nitrates or short-acting agents are common. α blockers are used for prevention in some patients.

**Extravasation of vasopressors**: phentolamine infiltrated subcutaneously around the site.

**Pheochromocytoma prep** (next lesson): phenoxybenzamine vs doxazosin; the choice depends on availability, cost and team experience.

**Prazosin for nightmares**: start low at bedtime and titrate; warn about first-dose orthostasis. Evidence is mixed; discuss expectations.

**Hypertensive emergency from catecholamine excess** (MAOI–tyramine reaction): phentolamine is the logical α blocker; never β blockade alone.

keyPoints: α1 blockers (-zosin): prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin for HTN and BPH; tamsulosin/silodosin α1A uroselective
First-dose orthostatic hypotension: start at bedtime, titrate
Tamsulosin → intraoperative floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery
Phenoxybenzamine: irreversible (covalent), nonselective; pheochromocytoma prep
Phentolamine: reversible nonselective; catecholamine crises, extravasation
Nonselective blockers cause more reflex tachycardia (α2 brake removed)

lessons.title: Beta Blockers: Classes and Properties

levels.kid:
**Beta blockers** cover the beta buttons that tell the heart to race and pump hard.

With the buttons covered, the heart beats slower and calmer, like a drummer who slows down the beat. That lowers blood pressure and gives a tired heart a rest.

Some beta blockers only cover the heart's buttons. Others also cover the buttons in the lungs, which can make breathing harder for people with asthma. Some sneak into the brain and can cause weird dreams. Doctors pick the right kind for each person, like choosing the right key for a lock.
levels.hs:
**β blockers** competitively block β receptors. Most end in **-olol**.

**Generations:**
- **Nonselective (β1 + β2)**: propranolol, nadolol, timolol, sotalol. Can tighten airways (β2 block).
- **β1-selective ("cardioselective")**: metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, betaxolol. Safer for the lungs, but selectivity fades at higher exposure.
- **Vasodilating**: **carvedilol** and **labetalol** also block α1; **nebivolol** is β1-selective and releases nitric oxide.

A memory trick: β1-selective drugs mostly start with **A–M** (acebutolol, atenolol, betaxolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, metoprolol); nonselective ones mostly with **N–Z** (nadolol, pindolol, propranolol, timolol). Nebivolol breaks the rule.

**Extra properties:**
- **Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA)**: pindolol and acebutolol partly stimulate the receptor, so the resting heart rate drops less.
- **Membrane-stabilizing (sodium channel) activity**: propranolol; this matters in overdose.
- **Lipophilic** (propranolol, metoprolol): cross into the brain → tiredness, vivid dreams; mostly cleared by the liver.
- **Hydrophilic** (atenolol, nadolol): stay out of the brain; cleared by the kidneys.
- **Esmolol** is broken down by blood esterases in minutes, so it can be adjusted quickly by IV infusion.
- **Sotalol** also blocks potassium channels (a class III antiarrhythmic).
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** β1 blockade lowers heart rate, contractility, AV conduction velocity and renin release; β2 blockade can cause bronchoconstriction, peripheral vasoconstriction, impaired hepatic glycogenolysis and reduced K+ uptake into cells. Many β blockers are **inverse agonists**, reducing constitutive receptor activity.

**Selectivity** is a ratio, not an absolute: bisoprolol and nebivolol are among the most β1-selective; metoprolol and atenolol are moderately selective. At higher concentrations all block β2.

**Ancillary properties:**
- **ISA (partial agonism)**: pindolol, acebutolol. Less resting bradycardia, less lipid change; avoided after MI and in heart failure because they lack proven mortality benefit.
- **Membrane stabilization**: propranolol (and acebutolol): Na+-channel block, relevant to QRS widening and seizures in overdose, irrelevant at therapeutic exposure.
- **α1 blockade**: carvedilol (β:α roughly 10:1) and labetalol (about 3:1 orally, about 7:1 IV) reduce SVR.
- **NO-mediated vasodilation**: nebivolol, via β3 agonism and endothelial NOS.
- **Class III action**: sotalol (hERG/IKr block) → QT prolongation and torsades risk.

**Pharmacokinetics:**
- Propranolol: highly lipophilic, extensive and variable first-pass metabolism (CYP2D6, CYP1A2), active metabolite.
- Metoprolol: CYP2D6 (poor metabolizers have higher levels and more bradycardia).
- Atenolol, nadolol, sotalol: renal excretion, long half-lives, accumulate in kidney disease.
- Esmolol: RBC esterase hydrolysis, half-life about nine minutes.
- Carvedilol: hepatic, take with food.

**Receptor adaptation**: chronic blockade upregulates β receptors, so abrupt withdrawal produces supersensitivity: rebound tachycardia, hypertension, angina or MI.
levels.phd:
**Inverse agonism and heart failure.** β1 receptors have constitutive (agonist-independent) activity, increased in failing myocardium. Inverse agonists such as metoprolol and carvedilol reduce this activity, whereas partial agonists (bucindolol has weak partial agonism; xamoterol is strongly partial) do not, which may explain why some β blockers failed in heart failure trials. The paradox of benefit from negative inotropes in a failing heart is resolved by chronic effects: reduced catecholamine toxicity (Ca2+ overload, apoptosis, CaMKII signaling), receptor resensitization, reversal of maladaptive remodeling and antiarrhythmic action.

**Biased ligands.** Carvedilol is a β-arrestin-biased ligand: it blocks Gs signaling while stimulating β-arrestin-dependent EGFR transactivation and ERK signaling in some cell systems. Whether this contributes to its clinical profile is debated; COMET (2003) found carvedilol reduced mortality more than metoprolol tartrate, though the metoprolol formulation and exposure were criticized.

**Stereochemistry.** Most β blockers are racemic; β-blocking activity resides largely in the (S)-enantiomer. Labetalol has two chiral centers and four stereoisomers with different α and β activities. Timolol and levobunolol are marketed as single enantiomers. Carvedilol's α1 blockade is shared by both enantiomers, but β blockade is mainly (S).

**Pharmacogenomics.** CYP2D6 poor metabolizers show several-fold higher metoprolol exposure; clinical guidelines (CPIC) suggest more cautious titration in them. ADRB1 Arg389Gly variants were linked to response to bucindolol in the BEST trial, an early example of genotype-guided cardiovascular therapy, though it has not entered routine care.

**Central effects.** Lipophilic β blockers penetrate the CNS; propranolol's effects on noradrenergic memory reconsolidation have been studied for anxiety and trauma, with mixed results.
levels.expert:
**Picking the β blocker is a practical problem.**

**Need it IV and titratable?** Esmolol: fast on, fast off, ideal for short procedures, aortic dissection initial control and post-craniotomy emergence hypertension and tachycardia. Labetalol: IV boluses or infusion, widely used for blood pressure control in intracerebral hemorrhage and stroke; it doesn't raise ICP because it doesn't dilate cerebral vessels the way nitroprusside does.

**Lung disease?** Cardioselective agents (bisoprolol, metoprolol) are tolerated by most patients with COPD and mild asthma, and the cardiac benefit usually outweighs the risk; avoid nonselective agents and propranolol in asthma.

**Kidney failure?** Prefer hepatically cleared agents (metoprolol, carvedilol); atenolol and sotalol accumulate.

**Heart failure with reduced EF?** Only three have mortality evidence: bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (extended release). Start low and titrate slowly once the patient is stable, not during acute decompensation.

**CNS side effects** (fatigue, sleep disturbance, nightmares)? Switch to a hydrophilic drug like atenolol, or take the drug in the morning.

**Neuro-specific:**
- **Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity** after severe TBI (episodes of tachycardia, hypertension, fever, sweating and posturing): nonselective, lipophilic propranolol is often chosen to block peripheral and central effects; gabapentin, clonidine and opioids are adjuncts.
- **Migraine and essential tremor**: propranolol (and metoprolol, timolol for migraine).
- Observational data link β blocker exposure after TBI to lower mortality; randomized trials are ongoing.

**Never stop abruptly** around surgery in patients taking them long term; perioperative withdrawal increases MI risk.

keyPoints: Nonselective: propranolol, nadolol, timolol, sotalol; β1-selective: atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, metoprolol (A–M)
Vasodilating: carvedilol and labetalol (α1 block), nebivolol (NO release)
ISA (pindolol, acebutolol): less bradycardia, not used post-MI or in HF
Propranolol: lipophilic, membrane-stabilizing (Na+ channel), CNS effects
Esmolol: RBC esterases, ultrashort; atenolol/nadolol/sotalol: renal
HFrEF mortality benefit: bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate only

lessons.title: Clinical Uses of Beta Blockers

levels.kid:
Beta blockers are like a calm coach for the heart. Doctors use them for lots of jobs.

They lower high blood pressure. They help hearts that hurt when they work too hard, because a slower heart needs less oxygen. After a heart attack, or when a heart is weak, they can help people live longer.

They also calm a shaky hand, help stop some headaches before they start, quiet a racing heart from a too-busy thyroid, and, as eye drops, lower pressure inside the eye. One medicine even helps shrink a kind of red birthmark in babies!
levels.hs:
**Heart and blood vessels:**
- **Angina**: slower heart rate and weaker squeeze → less oxygen demand.
- **After a heart attack**: reduce arrhythmias and reinfarction, especially when the heart is weakened.
- **Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction**: bisoprolol, carvedilol and metoprolol succinate help people live longer, started slowly once stable.
- **Arrhythmias**: control heart rate in atrial fibrillation; prevent some tachycardias.
- **High blood pressure**: effective, but usually not first choice unless there is another reason (like angina).
- **Aortic dissection**: lowering the force of each heartbeat protects the torn aorta.
- **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**: a slower heart fills better.

**Beyond the heart:**
- **Hyperthyroidism**: propranolol controls tremor, anxiety and racing heart while other treatment starts.
- **Migraine prevention**: propranolol, metoprolol, timolol.
- **Essential tremor**: propranolol.
- **Glaucoma**: timolol eye drops reduce fluid production in the eye.
- **Portal hypertension** in liver cirrhosis: nonselective β blockers (propranolol, nadolol, carvedilol) reduce bleeding from enlarged veins (varices).
- **Performance anxiety**: blocks the shaking and pounding heart.
- **Infantile hemangioma**: propranolol shrinks these birthmark tumors.
levels.college:
**Ischemic heart disease.** β1 blockade reduces heart rate, contractility and wall stress (lower myocardial O2 demand) and prolongs diastole (better coronary perfusion). They are first-line antianginals and were a cornerstone after MI based on pre-reperfusion era trials. Recent trials (REDUCE-AMI, 2024) found no benefit from routine β blockers after MI with preserved ejection fraction in the modern reperfusion era; benefit remains clear with reduced EF.

**HFrEF**: CIBIS-II (bisoprolol), MERIT-HF (metoprolol succinate) and COPERNICUS (carvedilol) each showed roughly a one-third mortality reduction. Mechanisms: reduced catecholamine toxicity, less arrhythmia, reverse remodeling. Initiate in euvolemic patients, titrate gradually; temporary worsening can occur.

**Arrhythmias**: class II antiarrhythmics slow SA firing and AV nodal conduction (rate control in AF and flutter); prevent catecholamine-triggered arrhythmias (long QT syndrome types 1 and 2, CPVT, where nadolol is preferred).

**Aortic dissection**: esmolol or labetalol first to reduce heart rate and dP/dt before adding vasodilators (which alone cause reflex tachycardia and more shear).

**Thyrotoxicosis**: propranolol blocks adrenergic symptoms and, at high exposure, reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion. It doesn't treat the gland.

**Portal hypertension**: β1 block lowers cardiac output; β2 block permits unopposed α splanchnic vasoconstriction, reducing portal inflow. Hence nonselective agents are required. Carvedilol adds α1-mediated intrahepatic resistance reduction.

**Neurology**: migraine prophylaxis (propranolol, metoprolol, timolol), essential tremor (propranolol, with primidone as the main alternative), akathisia (propranolol).

**Glaucoma**: timolol reduces aqueous humor production by ciliary epithelium β2 receptors; systemic absorption via the nasolacrimal duct can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm.
levels.phd:
**The hemangioma story** is a famous example of serendipity: in 2008, Léauté-Labrèze and colleagues noticed rapid regression of an infantile hemangioma in a child treated with propranolol for cardiomyopathy. Proposed mechanisms include vasoconstriction, reduced VEGF and bFGF signaling, induction of endothelial apoptosis, and an off-target action: (R)-propranolol, the "non-β-blocking" enantiomer, inhibits the transcription factor SOX18, which may explain efficacy independent of β blockade. A randomized trial (2015) confirmed efficacy, and propranolol became first-line.

**Cerebral cavernous malformations**: the same SOX18 and angiogenesis logic led to the TREAT_CCM pilot trial of propranolol for familial cavernous malformations, with inconclusive but interesting results. This is an active neurovascular research area.

**Memory reconsolidation**: propranolol given at memory reactivation reduced fear responses in some human studies (Kindt et al., 2009), but trials in PTSD show mixed results.

**Post-MI era effects.** Early trials (BHAT, 1981) predate reperfusion, statins and modern antiplatelet therapy. Infarct size, arrhythmic death and remodeling are now smaller, which shrinks the absolute benefit of β blockade in preserved EF. REDUCE-AMI and similar trials illustrate how a therapy's evidence base can age.

**Perioperative β blockade.** DECREASE trials promoted perioperative β blockers but were later discredited due to research misconduct; POISE (2008) showed that starting metoprolol right before noncardiac surgery reduced MI but increased stroke and death, likely from hypotension and bradycardia. The lesson: continue chronic β blockers but avoid starting them acutely just before surgery.

**Traumatic brain injury.** Catecholamine surges after TBI are linked to secondary brain injury and cardiac complications. Observational studies associate β blockers with lower mortality; pilot RCTs (for example of propranolol after severe TBI) are testing this.
levels.expert:
**How the clinician uses β blockers well.**

**Stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage**: labetalol (and nicardipine) are standard for rapid, controllable blood pressure lowering. In ICH, early intensive lowering (INTERACT trials) is common, avoiding big swings. In ischemic stroke before thrombolysis, there are blood pressure thresholds that must be met; labetalol is a typical first agent.

**Post-craniotomy and emergence**: esmolol and labetalol blunt the surge in heart rate and pressure that can provoke bleeding into the tumor bed.

**Subarachnoid hemorrhage**: catecholamine-driven arrhythmias and myocardial stunning are common. β blockers can protect the heart but can also lower blood pressure needed for brain perfusion; balance on an individual basis.

**Rate control in AF**: β blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. In AF with heart failure, prefer β blockers. Do not combine IV β blockers with IV verapamil or diltiazem (risk of profound AV block and asystole).

**Thyroid storm**: propranolol is classic (also reduces T4 to T3 conversion), with esmolol for unstable patients; it is part of a package with thionamides, iodine and steroids.

**Variceal bleeding prevention**: nonselective β blockers in cirrhosis. Watch for hypotension in refractory ascites or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

**Migraine and tremor**: propranolol works for both, but warn about fatigue, exercise intolerance, sexual side effects and depressed mood complaints (evidence for depression is weak). Avoid in asthma.

**Glaucoma drops**: always ask about timolol when a patient has unexplained bradycardia or wheeze: eye drops are systemic drugs.

**Aortic dissection**: get heart rate down first, then blood pressure.

keyPoints: Angina, HFrEF (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), rate control, post-MI with reduced EF
Aortic dissection: β blockade (esmolol/labetalol) before vasodilators
Thyrotoxicosis (propranolol), migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, akathisia

lessons.title: Adverse Effects and Contraindications

levels.kid:
Beta blockers are helpful, but they can cause problems too.

Because they slow the heart, sometimes they slow it **too much**, making people tired or dizzy. Some can tighten the air tubes in the lungs, which is bad for people with asthma. Hands and feet may feel cold.

For people with diabetes, low blood sugar usually makes the heart pound and hands shake, like an alarm. Beta blockers can turn that alarm down, so people might not notice.

And you should never stop them suddenly. The heart can bounce back racing too fast. Doctors lower them slowly instead.
levels.hs:
**Common adverse effects:**
- **Bradycardia** and heart block (slow heart, slowed signals).
- **Fatigue**, reduced exercise tolerance, cold hands and feet.
- **Bronchospasm** in asthma, especially with nonselective drugs.
- **Masking of hypoglycemia**: the warning signs of low blood sugar (pounding heart, tremor) are blunted. Sweating still happens, because sweat glands use acetylcholine.
- **Worsening acute heart failure** if started in a patient who is fluid-overloaded and decompensating.
- Sleep problems, vivid dreams (lipophilic drugs).
- Sexual side effects, and mood complaints (the link with depression is weak).

**Contraindications and cautions:**
- Severe bradycardia, high-grade heart block (without a pacemaker), cardiogenic shock, acute decompensated heart failure.
- Severe asthma (avoid nonselective drugs).
- **Cocaine- or pheochromocytoma-related hypertension**: β block alone can leave α constriction unopposed.
- Combining with **verapamil or diltiazem** → heart block.

**Withdrawal**: stopping suddenly can cause rebound tachycardia, high blood pressure, angina or even heart attack.

**Overdose**: very slow heart rate and low blood pressure, sometimes low blood sugar (especially in children), seizures and a wide QRS with propranolol. Treatment uses fluids, atropine, **glucagon**, calcium, **high-dose insulin** with glucose, vasopressors and pacing.
levels.college:
**Cardiac**: negative chronotropy and dromotropy → sinus bradycardia, AV block; caution in sick sinus syndrome. Negative inotropy can precipitate pulmonary edema in decompensated heart failure even though chronic use benefits HFrEF.

**Pulmonary**: β2 blockade removes bronchodilator tone. Cardioselective agents are generally tolerated in COPD and mild-to-moderate asthma (meta-analyses show small FEV1 changes), but nonselective agents, including topical timolol, can provoke severe bronchospasm.

**Metabolic**: blunted adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia and impaired glycogenolysis recovery (β2), particularly with nonselective agents in insulin-treated diabetes. Older agents can raise triglycerides and lower HDL modestly and slightly increase new-onset diabetes (atenolol with thiazide). Carvedilol and nebivolol are more metabolically neutral.

**Potassium**: β2 blockade reduces cellular K+ uptake → small serum K+ rise, relevant with exercise or in renal failure.

**Other**: peripheral vasoconstriction (Raynaud, claudication with nonselective drugs), psoriasis flares, fatigue.

**Anaphylaxis on β blockers**: reactions are more severe and resistant to epinephrine. **Glucagon** bypasses β receptors, activating adenylyl cyclase through its own Gs-coupled receptor.

**Overdose management** (poison center involved):
- Atropine for bradycardia (often insufficient).
- IV calcium and fluids.
- **High-dose insulin euglycemic therapy (HIET)**: improves myocardial carbohydrate use and contractility; glucose and potassium must be monitored closely.
- Glucagon (vomiting is common), catecholamines.
- Sodium bicarbonate for propranolol-induced QRS widening; benzodiazepines for seizures.
- Lipid emulsion for lipophilic agents (limited evidence), pacing, ECMO.
- Hemodialysis can remove hydrophilic, low protein-bound agents (atenolol, sotalol, nadolol).
- **Sotalol**: QT prolongation and torsades; magnesium and overdrive pacing.
levels.phd:
**Why β blockers mask but don't abolish hypoglycemia awareness.** Neurogenic symptoms of hypoglycemia include adrenergic (palpitations, tremor, anxiety) and cholinergic (sweating, hunger) components. β blockers blunt the adrenergic part; sweating is preserved via sympathetic cholinergic fibers. In insulin users, β2 blockade also impairs hepatic glycogenolysis and counterregulatory recovery. The clinical impact with cardioselective agents is modest, and diabetes is not a contraindication; impaired awareness of hypoglycemia is the real concern.

**The "unopposed α" controversy.** The idea that β blockade in cocaine toxicity or pheochromocytoma unmasks α vasoconstriction comes from case reports and small physiological studies. Retrospective studies of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain have not shown consistent harm from β blockers, and labetalol or carvedilol may avoid the issue. In pheochromocytoma, however, the risk is well established and β blockade must follow α blockade.

**Calcium channel blocker plus β blocker** toxicity: pharmacodynamic synergy at the SA and AV nodes and on contractility. Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) are safer partners because they act mainly on vessels.

**High-dose insulin mechanism.** In shock from β blocker or calcium channel blocker overdose, the myocardium shifts from fatty acid to carbohydrate use and becomes insulin resistant. Insulin at high exposure increases glucose uptake, myocardial energy and contractility, and improves microvascular perfusion; it acts within tens of minutes rather than immediately. Animal and human case series support it, and it is in consensus guidelines for calcium channel blocker poisoning.

**Erectile dysfunction and nocebo.** In one trial, men told about possible sexual side effects of atenolol reported far more dysfunction than men not told, illustrating nocebo effects; meta-analyses show only small absolute increases in sexual dysfunction with β blockers.

**Depression.** Large meta-analyses found no meaningful increase in depressive symptoms with β blockers, contradicting older teaching.
levels.expert:
**Senior clinician habits around β blocker safety.**

**Before starting**: heart rate and rhythm (look for AV block on the ECG), signs of decompensated heart failure, asthma history, concurrent nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers or digoxin, and in the elderly, falls and orthostasis.

**The patient who arrives bradycardic and hypotensive**: get the medication list, including eye drops and recent dose changes; check kidney function (atenolol and sotalol accumulate), potassium and glucose. In older patients, a new kidney injury plus atenolol and a calcium channel blocker is a common recipe for "BRASH" (bradycardia, renal failure, AV nodal blockade, shock, hyperkalemia): treat all five components together.

**Anaphylaxis in a patient on a β blocker**: epinephrine still first; if refractory, glucagon; avoid labeling the patient as epinephrine-resistant too early.

**Neurology and neurosurgery angles:**
- **Myasthenia gravis**: β blockers (including timolol drops) can worsen weakness; use with caution.
- **Stroke patients**: avoid aggressive β blockade that drops cerebral perfusion in patients dependent on blood pressure (for example with severe carotid stenosis).
- **Seizures and wide QRS** in a propranolol overdose look like a primary neurological emergency; the ECG and the history make the diagnosis. Benzodiazepines and bicarbonate, not phenytoin.
- After **SAH**, sudden bradycardia may come from raised ICP (Cushing response) rather than medication; check the patient, not just the drug chart.

**Perioperative**: continue chronic β blockers, including on the morning of surgery; don't start them the day before surgery.

**Stopping**: taper over one to two weeks in patients with coronary disease.

keyPoints: Bradycardia, AV block, fatigue, cold extremities, bronchospasm (nonselective worse)
Mask adrenergic hypoglycemia symptoms; sweating is preserved
Contraindicated in acute decompensated HF, high-grade AV block, cardiogenic shock
Never β-block first in pheochromocytoma; avoid IV combination with verapamil/diltiazem
Abrupt withdrawal → rebound tachycardia, angina, MI; taper
Overdose: atropine, calcium, glucagon, high-dose insulin euglycemia, pressors, pacing; dialysis for atenolol/sotalol/nadolol

lessons.title: Pheochromocytoma Pharmacology

levels.kid:
A **pheochromocytoma** is a rare lump that grows in the adrenal gland, the little hat on top of each kidney. The lump makes way too much adrenaline-type messenger.

So the person gets sudden attacks: a pounding headache, sweating, a racing heart and very high blood pressure.

Surgeons take the lump out, but first doctors give medicines for a week or two to calm things down. The order matters a lot: first a medicine that relaxes the blood vessels, and only after that a medicine that slows the heart. Doing it the other way around could make blood pressure shoot up dangerously.
levels.hs:
**Pheochromocytoma** is a tumor of chromaffin cells in the **adrenal medulla** that releases catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, sometimes dopamine). Similar tumors outside the adrenal are called **paragangliomas**.

**Symptoms**: episodes of **headache, sweating and palpitations** (the classic triad) with high blood pressure. Pressure on the tumor, anesthesia and some medicines can trigger attacks.

**Diagnosis**: measure **metanephrines** (catecholamine breakdown products) in plasma or urine, then image the tumor with CT or MRI.

**Getting ready for surgery** (usually one to two weeks):
1. **α blocker first**: **phenoxybenzamine** (irreversible) or **doxazosin** (selective α1). This relaxes blood vessels and controls blood pressure.
2. **Fluids and salt**: the chronically squeezed vessels have a low blood volume; refilling it prevents a crash after the tumor is removed.
3. **β blocker only after α blockade** to control a fast heart rate.
- **Never give a β blocker first**: blocking β2 vasodilation leaves α constriction unopposed, and blood pressure can spike.
- Extra options: calcium channel blockers, and **metyrosine**, which blocks catecholamine production.

**During surgery**: touching the tumor causes surges, treated with fast IV drugs such as phentolamine, nitroprusside or nicardipine. After the tumor's veins are tied off, blood pressure can drop sharply and blood sugar can fall.

About a third or more of these tumors are linked to inherited genes, so genetic testing is recommended.
levels.college:
**Biochemistry.** Chromaffin tumors synthesize catecholamines and continuously metabolize them inside the tumor via **COMT** to metanephrine and normetanephrine. Because this intratumoral conversion is constant even between paroxysms, **plasma free metanephrines** (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines) are the most sensitive tests. False positives: tricyclic antidepressants, phenoxybenzamine, SNRIs, MAO inhibitors, levodopa, stress and sampling while seated. Tumors with no PNMT (most paragangliomas) secrete mainly NE; adrenal tumors may secrete Epi.

**Preoperative blockade:**
- **Phenoxybenzamine**: noncompetitive (covalent) α1/α2 block that a catecholamine surge can't overcome. Downsides: reflex tachycardia (α2 block), orthostatic hypotension, nasal congestion, and prolonged postoperative hypotension.
- **Doxazosin/prazosin/terazosin**: competitive α1 block, less tachycardia, shorter acting. The PRESCRIPT trial (2020) found no difference in the primary outcome of intraoperative hemodynamic instability time between phenoxybenzamine and doxazosin, though phenoxybenzamine gave somewhat better control.
- **Calcium channel blockers** (nicardipine, amlodipine) as add-on or alternatives.
- **β blockers** after adequate α blockade (several days) for tachycardia. Labetalol is a poor initial choice because its β:α ratio favors β.
- **Metyrosine** (α-methyl-para-tyrosine) inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase; side effects: sedation, depression, extrapyramidal symptoms, crystalluria.

**Drugs that can precipitate crises**: β blockers without α blockade, **metoclopramide** and other D2 antagonists, glucagon, corticosteroids (high exposure), sympathomimetics, MAO inhibitors, tricyclics, opioids that release histamine, and some neuromuscular blockers that release histamine.

**After tumor removal**: catecholamine withdrawal plus residual α blockade and downregulated receptors → hypotension needing fluids and vasopressors; rebound hyperinsulinemia → hypoglycemia (monitor glucose for a day).
levels.phd:
**Genetics reshaped the field.** The old "rule of 10s" (10% bilateral, malignant, familial, extra-adrenal) is outdated: about 35–40% of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas carry germline mutations, the highest heritability of any human tumor. Molecular clusters:
- **Cluster 1 (pseudohypoxia)**: SDHx, VHL, EPAS1 (HIF-2α), FH. Noradrenergic phenotype, often extra-adrenal; SDHB carries the highest metastatic risk.
- **Cluster 2 (kinase signaling)**: RET (MEN2), NF1, TMEM127, MAX. Adrenergic phenotype (express PNMT), mostly adrenal.
- **Cluster 3 (Wnt signaling)**: somatic CSDE1 and MAML3 fusions.

**Biochemical phenotype predicts genotype**: high normetanephrine with low metanephrine suggests cluster 1; raised **3-methoxytyramine** (dopamine metabolite) points to SDHx and higher metastatic risk.

**Pseudohypoxia therapeutics**: HIF-2α stabilization drives cluster 1 tumors, and the HIF-2α inhibitor **belzutifan**, developed for von Hippel–Lindau disease, has shown activity in advanced pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma and has entered use for this indication.

**Functional imaging**: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET (somatostatin receptors) is highly sensitive for SDHx-related and head-and-neck paragangliomas; 18F-DOPA PET for others; MIBG scintigraphy exploits uptake via NET, the same transporter discussed with indirect sympathomimetics, making radiolabeled MIBG a "Trojan horse" therapy for metastatic disease.

**Why α before β is physiology, not dogma**: with high circulating Epi, β2-mediated skeletal muscle vasodilation partially offsets α1 vasoconstriction. Removing it with β blockade shifts the balance to unopposed α1, raising afterload acutely; in catecholamine cardiomyopathy this can precipitate pulmonary edema. Whether selective β1 blockade alone is as dangerous is debated, but the consensus sequence remains.
levels.expert:
**Why a neurosurgeon cares.**

**Head and neck paragangliomas** (carotid body tumors, glomus jugulare and glomus vagale) sit right in skull-base neurosurgical territory. Most are parasympathetic and nonsecretory, but a minority secrete catecholamines, and SDHx carriers can have multiple tumors, including an unsuspected adrenal pheochromocytoma. Screen with plasma metanephrines before surgery or embolization; a hypertensive crisis during skull-base surgery is an avoidable disaster.

**Headache plus hypertension** in a young patient: pheochromocytoma belongs on the differential with intracranial causes such as reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) and hypertensive encephalopathy. Pheochromocytoma crisis can cause intracerebral hemorrhage, PRES, seizures and stroke. Before giving metoclopramide for a "migraine" with severe hypertension, think twice.

**Neurocutaneous syndromes**: NF1 and von Hippel–Lindau disease (cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas) carry pheochromocytoma risk. A VHL patient going for posterior fossa surgery needs biochemical screening first.

**Perioperative checklist with the anesthesia team:**
- Adequate α blockade: blood pressure controlled, mild orthostasis, nasal stuffiness suggest effect.
- Volume expansion with liberal salt and fluids.
- β blockade only after α.
- Arterial line before induction; short-acting vasodilators (nitroprusside, nicardipine, clevidipine, phentolamine), esmolol and magnesium prepared.
- Avoid triggers: metoclopramide, droperidol, histamine-releasing drugs, ephedrine, succinylcholine fasciculations pressing on an abdominal tumor (debated).
- After venous ligation: norepinephrine or vasopressin ready, and glucose checks.

**Pregnancy** with undiagnosed pheochromocytoma has high maternal and fetal mortality; α blockade first, timing of surgery by trimester, a multidisciplinary call.

**Lifelong follow-up** with metanephrines, because recurrences and new tumors occur, especially in germline carriers.

keyPoints: Chromaffin tumor of adrenal medulla (paraganglioma if extra-adrenal); triad: headache, sweating, palpitations
Diagnose with plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines (continuous intratumoral COMT metabolism)
Preop: α blockade first (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) + volume expansion, then β blockade
Never β first: unopposed α → hypertensive crisis; metoclopramide can trigger crises
Metyrosine inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase; post-resection hypotension and hypoglycemia
About 35–40% germline: SDHx (SDHB metastatic), VHL, RET, NF1; screen skull-base paragangliomas before surgery
